definition: Reverent means showing deep, awed respect — treating something as near-sacred in how you speak, move, or stay silent before it.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word reverent. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know reverent should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The apprentice lifted the old luthier's violin with reverent care, as though a careless breath could crack it.
Respectful is milder than reverent: a respectful visitor follows the rules and keeps a polite tone, while a reverent one is quieted by genuine awe.
Worshipful goes further than reverent — reverent respect keeps a human distance, while worshipful devotion treats its object as divine.

Respectful is the everyday, all-purpose word — polite and considerate toward anyone, in any setting — and it asks nothing more of you than good manners. Reverent goes much further: the respect deepens into awe, is saved for what feels close to sacred, and shows in hushed voices and careful hands.

Solemn describes the weight of a mood or occasion — grave, formal, no lightness anywhere — without pointing at anything. Reverent is aimed: deep respect directed at one particular thing held in awe. A judge can be solemn all day out of habit; a person is reverent only before something.

Reverent is the exact word for that hush, because it means showing deep, awed respect — treating something as near-sacred in how you speak, move, or stay silent before it.
Nobody instructed the group; the awe did.
A respectful group would have kept the trail rules and the noise down, and thought no more about it; a reverent one lowers its voice the way people do in front of something they cannot quite measure.

Keep its neighbors straight — respectful is everyday courtesy with no awe in it; solemn is gravity of mood that points at nothing in particular; reverent is respect deepened into awe and aimed at something held near-sacred.
Two traps ride along with this word: the sound-alike reverie is a daydream, no relation at all, and the re- up front is an intensifier — a reverent hush is not a hush that happens again.

The trail into the Calaveras grove passes a sign that gives no rules; it says only, 'You are entering the presence of the oldest living things you will ever meet.' Ranger Delia Vasquez has watched the same change come over visitors for twenty years.
Loud families go quiet at the first big trunk.
Hikers take off their hats without being asked, and voices drop to the level of a library, or lower.
She calls it the reverent hush: people are not afraid, and they are not praying -- they stand with their heads back, careful even about where they put their feet.
The grove has no guards and no fences, she points out, and in twenty years no one has carved so much as an initial.
